ISO 26262: what are the technical requirements for the functional requirement "Display shall be able to receive data from HMI and show it"?
answer:
# ISO 26262 Technical Requirements for Display Data Reception and Visualization

## Context & ASIL Determination

Before defining technical requirements, you need to establish:
- **ASIL level** (A–D) based on Severity × Exposure × Controllability
- **Item definition** and **hazard analysis & risk assessment (HARA)**
- **Functional safety concept** derived from HARA

---

## Technical Safety Requirements (TSRs)

### 1. 📡 Data Reception Requirements

| Requirement | Technical Specification |
|---|---|
| **Communication Interface** | Display shall support defined interface (e.g., SPI, CAN, LVDS, Ethernet) with specified baud rate/bandwidth |
| **Message Integrity** | Data frames shall include CRC/checksum (e.g., CRC-8/16/32 per ASIL level) |
| **Message Counter** | Rolling counter shall be implemented to detect lost/repeated messages |
| **Timeout Detection** | Display shall detect communication loss within defined time window (e.g., ≤ 100ms) |
| **Signal Range Check** | Received data shall be validated against min/max plausible range |

---

### 2. 🖥️ Display Rendering Requirements

| Requirement | Technical Specification |
|---|---|
| **Latency** | End-to-end latency from data reception to display update shall be ≤ defined value (e.g., ≤ 200ms) |
| **Refresh Rate** | Display shall update at minimum defined frame rate (e.g., ≥ 30Hz for dynamic content) |
| **Pixel Accuracy** | Rendered values shall match received data within defined tolerance |
| **Resolution** | Minimum resolution shall meet readability requirements under defined conditions |
| **Luminance/Contrast** | Display shall maintain readability under all lighting conditions (e.g., direct sunlight) |

---

### 3. ⚠️ Failure Detection & Handling

| Requirement | Technical Specification |
|---|---|
| **Black Screen Detection** | Display shall detect and report complete loss of output within defined time |
| **Frozen Image Detection** | Display watchdog shall detect static/frozen image (e.g., same frame for > 500ms) |
| **Backlight Failure** | Backlight failure shall be detected and a safe state triggered |
| **Safe State** | Upon failure detection, display shall transition to safe state (e.g., show warning, go blank with indicator) |
| **Error Notification** | Detected faults shall be reported to HMI/supervising ECU via diagnostic interface |

---

### 4. 🔒 Functional Safety Mechanisms (per ASIL)

```
ASIL A:
  └── Basic CRC + plausibility check

ASIL B:
  └── CRC + message counter + timeout monitoring

ASIL C:
  └── Above + redundant signal paths + end-to-end protection (E2E Profile)

ASIL D:
  └── Above + hardware redundancy + independent monitoring channel
       + periodic self-test of display hardware
```

> **E2E Protection:** Commonly implemented per **AUTOSAR E2E Profiles** (Profile 1–7) depending on ASIL level

---

### 5. 🔁 Self-Test Requirements

| Requirement | Description |
|---|---|
| **Power-on Self-Test (POST)** | Display hardware integrity verified at startup |
| **Runtime Monitoring** | Continuous or periodic pixel/GPU/memory self-check |
| **Diagnostic Coverage (DC)** | Shall meet minimum DC per ASIL (e.g., DC ≥ 90% for ASIL C/D) |
| **FTTI Compliance** | Fault detection shall occur within Fault Tolerant Time Interval defined in safety concept |

---

### 6. 🌡️ Environmental & Hardware Requirements

| Requirement | Specification |
|---|---|
| **Operating Temperature** | e.g., −40°C to +85°C (AEC-Q100 Grade 1) |
| **Voltage Supply Monitoring** | Under/overvoltage detection with safe state transition |
| **EMC Compliance** | Shall meet CISPR 25, ISO 11452 requirements |
| **Vibration/Shock** | Shall comply with ISO 16750-3 |

---

### 7. 📋 Derived Hardware Safety Requirements (DHSR)

Per **ISO 26262-5**, hardware must meet:

```
- PMHF (Probabilistic Metric for Hardware Failures):
    ASIL B: < 10⁻⁷ h⁻¹
    ASIL C: < 10⁻⁷ h⁻¹
    ASIL D: < 10⁻⁸ h⁻¹

- Single Point Fault Metric (SPFM):
    ASIL C: ≥ 90%
    ASIL D: ≥ 99%

- Latent Fault Metric (LFM):
    ASIL C: ≥ 60%
    ASIL D: ≥ 90%
```

---

## Summary Flow

```
Functional Requirement
        │
        ▼
  HARA → ASIL Assignment
        │
        ▼
  Functional Safety Requirement (FSR)
        │
        ▼
  Technical Safety Requirement (TSR)
  ┌─────┴──────────────────────────┐
  │  - Data integrity (CRC, E2E)   │
  │  - Latency & refresh rate      │
  │  - Failure detection           │
  │  - Safe state behavior         │
  │  - Self-test coverage          │
  │  - Hardware metrics (PMHF)     │
  └────────────────────────────────┘
```

---

## ⚠️ Key Note

> The exact technical requirements **depend heavily on the ASIL level assigned** during HARA. A display showing **vehicle speed** (safety-critical) may be **ASIL B/C**, while infotainment content may be **QM (Quality Management)** — requiring very different rigor.

text: ISO 26262: technical requiremen for functional requirement "HMI shall enable driver display to detect HU malfunctions"
answer:
# ISO 26262 Technical Requirements for HMI Malfunction Detection

## Functional Requirement Analysis

**Parent Functional Requirement:**
> *"HMI shall enable driver display to detect HU (Head Unit) malfunctions"*

---

## 1. ASIL Determination Considerations

| Parameter | Assessment |
|-----------|------------|
| **Severity (S)** | S1–S2 (Driver distraction / loss of safety-relevant information) |
| **Exposure (E)** | E4 (Continuous driving operation) |
| **Controllability (C)** | C2–C3 (Driver may not notice silent failure) |
| **Likely ASIL** | **ASIL A – ASIL B** (depending on HU safety functions displayed) |

> ⚠️ If HU controls **safety-critical functions** (e.g., ADAS, parking assist), ASIL could escalate to **ASIL C/D**

---

## 2. Derived Technical Safety Requirements (TSR)

### 2.1 Malfunction Detection Requirements

```
TSR-01: The driver display shall monitor HU heartbeat/alive signal
        at a maximum interval of [X ms] (typically ≤ 100ms)

TSR-02: The driver display shall detect loss of communication with
        HU within [X ms] of failure occurrence (≤ 500ms recommended)

TSR-03: The display system shall detect HU internal errors via
        dedicated diagnostic status messages (e.g., over E2E protected
        communication channel)

TSR-04: The system shall distinguish between:
        (a) HU communication loss
        (b) HU processing fault
        (c) HU power supply fault
        (d) HU software fault
```

### 2.2 Diagnostic Coverage Requirements

```
TSR-05: End-to-End (E2E) protection shall be implemented on
        HU→Display communication (ISO 26262-6, E2E Library)
        - CRC protection
        - Message counter
        - Sequence monitoring

TSR-06: Diagnostic Coverage (DC) shall meet:
        - Single-point fault metric per ASIL level
        - ASIL A: DC ≥ 60% (low)
        - ASIL B: DC ≥ 90% (medium/high)

TSR-07: Hardware diagnostic shall include:
        - Watchdog monitoring of HU processor
        - Voltage monitoring of HU power rails
        - Memory integrity check (ECC/CRC)
```

### 2.3 Notification/Warning Requirements

```
TSR-08: Upon detection of HU malfunction, a visual warning
        shall be displayed within ≤ [X ms] (e.g., ≤ 500ms)

TSR-09: Warning indication shall be:
        - Unambiguous and clearly visible (luminance/contrast per
          ISO 15008 or OEM HMI standards)
        - Persistent until fault is cleared or acknowledged

TSR-10: Audible warning shall accompany visual warning if
        HU controls safety-relevant functions (per OEM requirement)

TSR-11: Warning message shall provide sufficient information
        to guide driver action (safe state guidance)
```

### 2.4 Safe State Requirements

```
TSR-12: On detection of HU malfunction, the system shall
        transition to a defined safe state within
        FTTI (Fault Tolerant Time Interval)

TSR-13: Safe state shall include:
        - Display of last known safe status OR
        - Display of default/fallback warning screen

TSR-14: Safety-critical HU functions shall fall back to
        independent hardware path (independence from HU)
```

---

## 3. Communication Architecture Requirements

```
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                 Technical Requirements               │
│                                                     │
│  HU ──[E2E Protected CAN/Ethernet]──► Display ECU  │
│         │                                           │
│         ├─ Alive Counter (1–15, rolling)            │
│         ├─ CRC-8/CRC-32 per E2E Profile             │
│         ├─ Diagnostic Status Byte                   │
│         └─ Heartbeat Signal (cyclic, e.g., 10ms)   │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

| Communication Req. | Specification |
|-------------------|---------------|
| **Protocol** | CAN FD / Automotive Ethernet |
| **E2E Profile** | E2E Profile 2, 4, or 7 (AUTOSAR) |
| **Cycle Time** | ≤ 10–50 ms (ASIL-dependent) |
| **Timeout Detection** | ≤ 3 missed frames → fault declared |
| **Error Counter** | Threshold-based fault confirmation |

---

## 4. Verification & Validation Requirements

### 4.1 Test Requirements

| Test Type | Requirement |
|-----------|-------------|
| **Fault Injection** | Simulate HU communication loss → verify display response |
| **Timing Test** | Verify detection latency ≤ defined FTTI |
| **E2E Test** | Corrupt CRC/counter → verify fault detection |
| **Power Fail Test** | Remove HU power → verify display warning activation |
| **Boundary Test** | Verify behavior at min/max fault thresholds |

### 4.2 Metrics to Be Demonstrated

```
□ PMHF (Probabilistic Metric for Hardware Failures) < target
□ Single Point Fault Metric (SPFM) ≥ ASIL target
□ Latent Fault Metric (LFM) ≥ ASIL target
□ DC (Diagnostic Coverage) ≥ ASIL target
```

---

## 5. ISO 26262 Reference Clauses

| Clause | Relevance |
|--------|-----------|
| **ISO 26262-3** | Item definition, HARA |
| **ISO 26262-4** | TSR derivation from FSR |
| **ISO 26262-5** | Hardware diagnostic requirements |
| **ISO 26262-6** | Software E2E implementation |
| **ISO 26262-9** | ASIL decomposition (if applied) |
| **ISO 26262-11** | Semiconductor/SoC requirements for display |

---

## 6. Summary Requirement Table

| ID | Technical Requirement | ASIL | Verification Method |
|----|----------------------|------|---------------------|
| TSR-01 | HU heartbeat monitoring ≤ 100ms | A/B | Test |
| TSR-02 | Communication loss detection ≤ 500ms | A/B | Test + Analysis |
| TSR-03 | E2E protection on HU-Display link | A/B | Review + Test |
| TSR-04 | Fault classification (4 types) | A/B | Test |
| TSR-05 | CRC + Counter on messages | A/B | Review + Test |
| TSR-08 | Warning display ≤ 500ms | A/B | Test |
| TSR-12 | Safe state transition within FTTI | A/B | Test + Analysis |

---

> **Note:** All timing values (X ms) shall be derived from **FTTI analysis** during the HARA phase and confirmed through **DFA (Dependent Failure Analysis)** and **FMEA/FTA** at system level.

text: ISO 26262:  Test Specification for a functional requirement "HMI-Driver-Display shall be able to detect errors or unplausible data in the data stream and show a warning on Driver-Display". Write only a expected result
answer:
# ISO 26262 Test Specification – Expected Results

**Functional Requirement:** *HMI-Driver-Display shall be able to detect errors or implausible data in the data stream and show a warning on Driver-Display*

---

## Expected Results

### TC-001 | Detection of Corrupted Data in the Data Stream
> The Driver-Display **shall detect** the corrupted/invalid data within **≤ [X] ms** of occurrence and **shall not render** any incorrect or misleading information on the display.

---

### TC-002 | Display of Warning Message upon Error Detection
> Upon detection of an error or implausible data, the Driver-Display **shall present a clearly visible warning indicator/message** to the driver within **≤ [X] ms**, conforming to the defined warning presentation requirements (position, color, symbol, and priority level).

---

### TC-003 | Warning Persistence During Ongoing Error Condition
> The warning **shall remain continuously visible** on the Driver-Display for the entire duration of the error or implausible data condition, without flickering, disappearing, or being overridden by lower-priority display content.

---

### TC-004 | Warning Dismissal upon Recovery of Valid Data
> Once valid and plausible data is restored to the data stream, the warning **shall be cleared** from the Driver-Display within **≤ [X] ms**, and normal display operation **shall resume** without residual error indications.

---

### TC-005 | Handling of Missing / No Data (Signal Timeout)
> When no data is received within the defined timeout threshold **[X] ms**, the Driver-Display **shall detect the signal loss**, **shall not display** the last known (stale) value as current, and **shall activate** the corresponding warning on the display.

---

### TC-006 | Implausible Data Detection (Out-of-Range Values)
> When data values exceed the defined valid range **[Min – Max]**, the Driver-Display **shall identify** the data as implausible, **shall suppress** the implausible value from being shown, and **shall display** the warning to the driver.

---

### TC-007 | Simultaneous Multiple Error Conditions
> When multiple errors or implausible data conditions occur simultaneously, the Driver-Display **shall detect all active errors** and **shall display warnings** according to the defined priority scheme, ensuring **no warning is suppressed** without a documented priority rationale.

---

### TC-008 | Warning Display under Degraded System Conditions
> Under degraded system conditions (e.g., reduced voltage, high temperature), the Driver-Display **shall still detect** errors or implausible data and **shall correctly render** the warning without loss of visibility or functionality, meeting the ASIL-defined availability requirements.

---

### TC-009 | No False Warning (No Fault Injected)
> When valid and plausible data is continuously present in the data stream, the Driver-Display **shall not generate or display** any warning indication, confirming **no false-positive** warning behavior.

---

### TC-010 | Warning Reaction Time (Latency Verification)
> The end-to-end latency from error/implausible data occurrence in the data stream to the warning being **visually confirmed on the Driver-Display shall not exceed [X] ms**, as defined by the system timing requirement and ASIL decomposition.

---

**Note:** All expected results shall be verified against the applicable ASIL level, and evidence shall be traceable to the safety goal and functional safety requirement as per **ISO 26262-6**.

text: ISO 26262: Test Specification for the Technical Requirement "CAN Interface  shall ensure that all received signals are forwarded to their destination"? Write only test procedure!
answer:
# Test Specification: CAN Interface Signal Forwarding

## Test Procedure

---

### TP-CAN-FWD-001: Nominal Signal Forwarding – Single Signal

**Objective:** Verify that a single received CAN signal is correctly forwarded to its defined destination.

**Preconditions:**
- DUT is powered and initialized
- CAN bus is operational (no bus-off, no error-passive state)
- Test equipment (CANoe/CANalyzer or equivalent) connected to CAN bus
- Destination interface (memory, SW component, actuator interface) is accessible for readback

**Steps:**
1. Configure test tool to transmit a CAN message with a defined signal value (e.g., Signal_A = 0x55) on the configured CAN ID.
2. Trigger transmission of the CAN message on the bus.
3. Wait for the defined processing cycle (≤ defined forwarding latency).
4. Read back the signal value at the defined destination (e.g., internal RAM variable, RTE port, output CAN message).
5. Compare the received signal value at the destination with the transmitted value.

**Expected Result:**
- Signal value at destination equals transmitted value (0x55).
- No signal loss or corruption observed.
- Forwarding occurs within the specified latency.

---

### TP-CAN-FWD-002: Nominal Signal Forwarding – All Defined Signals (Full Coverage)

**Objective:** Verify that **all** signals defined in the CAN communication matrix (DBC/ARXML) are forwarded to their respective destinations.

**Preconditions:**
- Complete CAN database (DBC/ARXML) loaded into test tool
- All signal-to-destination mappings documented in the Signal Routing Table
- DUT is fully initialized

**Steps:**
1. Load the complete CAN signal routing table (source CAN ID + signal name → destination).
2. For each signal defined in the routing table:
   a. Transmit the CAN message containing the signal with a defined test value (e.g., minimum valid value).
   b. Wait for forwarding cycle to complete.
   c. Read back the value at the defined destination.
   d. Log result (PASS/FAIL) per signal.
3. Repeat Step 2 for maximum valid value for each signal.
4. Generate test report listing all signals with forwarding status.

**Expected Result:**
- 100% of signals defined in the routing table are forwarded to their correct destination.
- All read-back values match transmitted values.
- No signal is missing or routed to an incorrect destination.

---

### TP-CAN-FWD-003: Signal Forwarding Under Continuous Bus Load

**Objective:** Verify signal forwarding under high CAN bus load conditions.

**Preconditions:**
- CAN bus load generator configured to produce ≥ 80% bus load with background traffic
- DUT operational

**Steps:**
1. Start CAN bus load generator to simulate ≥ 80% bus load.
2. Transmit target CAN messages containing all signals under test at their nominal cycle time.
3. Monitor destination interfaces for all expected forwarded signal values over a period of 60 seconds.
4. Record any missed forwarding events, delayed forwarding, or corrupted values.
5. Stop bus load generator.
6. Evaluate results against specification (latency, completeness).

**Expected Result:**
- All signals are forwarded to destinations without loss.
- Forwarding latency does not exceed the specified maximum under high bus load.
- No signal corruption observed.

---

### TP-CAN-FWD-004: Signal Forwarding After CAN Bus Recovery (Bus-Off Recovery)

**Objective:** Verify that signal forwarding resumes correctly after CAN bus-off recovery.

**Preconditions:**
- DUT operational and forwarding signals nominally
- Capability to inject bus errors (e.g., CANstress or equivalent tool)

**Steps:**
1. Confirm all signals are being forwarded nominally (baseline check).
2. Inject CAN bus errors to force the DUT CAN controller into bus-off state.
3. Verify DUT enters bus-off state (monitor via diagnostic or status register).
4. Remove error injection and allow DUT to perform bus-off recovery (per ISO 11898).
5. After recovery confirmation, transmit all defined CAN messages with known signal values.
6. Read back all signal values at their defined destinations.
7. Compare read-back values with transmitted values.

**Expected Result:**
- DUT recovers from bus-off state within specified recovery time.
- All signals are correctly forwarded after recovery.
- No permanent loss of signal forwarding observed.

---

### TP-CAN-FWD-005: Signal Forwarding Integrity – Boundary Values

**Objective:** Verify that signals are forwarded correctly for boundary (minimum and maximum) raw values.

**Preconditions:**
- Signal value ranges defined in DBC/ARXML
- DUT operational

**Steps:**
1. For each signal under test:
   a. Transmit the signal with raw value = **minimum** valid value.
   b. Read back value at destination.
   c. Verify value matches.
   d. Transmit the signal with raw value = **maximum** valid value.
   e. Read back value at destination.
   f. Verify value matches.
   g. Transmit the signal with raw value = **0x00** (zero).
   h. Read back value at destination.
   i. Verify value matches.

**Expected Result:**
- All boundary values are forwarded without modification, truncation, or corruption.

---

### TP-CAN-FWD-006: Signal Forwarding Latency Measurement

**Objective:** Verify that signal forwarding latency is within the specified maximum latency.

**Preconditions:**
- Timestamp capability available on both CAN reception and destination readback
- Maximum forwarding latency specified (e.g., T_max = X ms)

**Steps:**

Myanmar for the construction and operation of a Multimodal Transit Transport Facility on
Kaladan river connecting the Sittwe port in Myanmar with the state of Mizoram in India. The port
connects to Paletwa in Myanmar through an inland waterway and from Paletwa to Zorinpui in
Mizoram through a road component. Once fully operationalised, KMTTP will provide alternate
connectivity from Eastern coast of India to the North-eastern states through the Sittwe port. The

answer:
# India Inaugurates Sittwe Port Operations, Boosting Connectivity to Northeast

**A Historic Step Forward for the Kaladan Multimodal Transit Transport Project**

**Kolkata, May 2023** — In a significant development for India-Myanmar bilateral relations and regional connectivity, Minister of State for Ports, Shipping and Waterways, NAME_1, on Wednesday flagged off vessel MV-ITT LION (V-273) from Syama Prasad Mookerjee Port in Kolkata, marking the inaugural shipment to operationalise the newly developed Sittwe Port in the Rakhine State of Myanmar.

The vessel, carrying 20,000 bags of cement totalling 1,000 metric tonnes, is expected to arrive at Sittwe Port on **May 9, 2023**, officially launching commercial operations at the facility.

## A Project Years in the Making

Sittwe Port has been constructed under a **grant assistance from the Government of India** as part of the ambitious **Kaladan Multimodal Transit Transport Project (KMTTP)**. The Inland Waterways Authority of India (IWAI), serving as the Project Development Consultant, has successfully overseen the implementation of both the port and inland waterway transport components of the project.

The port was developed under a framework agreement between India and Myanmar for the establishment of a Multimodal Transit Transport Facility along the Kaladan River, creating a vital link between Sittwe and the northeastern Indian state of **Mizoram**.

## A Gateway to Northeast India

The KMTTP represents a strategic infrastructure corridor connecting multiple transport modes:

- **Sea route** from Eastern India to Sittwe Port
- **Inland waterway** connecting Sittwe to Paletwa in Myanmar
- **Road corridor** from Paletwa to Zorinpui in Mizoram

Once fully operationalised, the project will provide an **alternate connectivity route** from India's Eastern coast to its landlocked northeastern states, significantly reducing the dependence on the narrow Siliguri Corridor, also known as the "Chicken's Neck."

## Broader Regional Impact

Officials believe the operationalisation of Sittwe Port will unlock enormous economic potential for the region. The port is expected to open new trade and transit opportunities to and from Myanmar, particularly benefiting the **Rakhine State**, while further strengthening trade and commerce between the two neighbouring countries and the broader Southeast Asian region.

The successful completion of this project underscores India's commitment to its **"Neighbourhood First" and "Act East" policies**, reinforcing its strategic and economic partnerships with Myanmar and the wider region.

---
*Reporting by our correspondent | Kolkata Bureau*

text: In this paper, based on the physically neutral plane, the PDDO method is used to study the dimensionless frequencies and modes of porous functionally graded thin plates under four pore distributions.
answer:
# Peridynamic Differential Operator (PDDO) Analysis of Porous Functionally Graded Thin Plates

## Overview

This paper presents a **Peridynamic Differential Operator (PDDO)**-based methodology for analyzing the free vibration characteristics of porous functionally graded (FG) thin plates, incorporating the concept of the **physically neutral plane** under four distinct pore distribution patterns.

---

## Key Theoretical Framework

### 1. Physically Neutral Plane Concept

The neutral plane position is determined by eliminating membrane-bending coupling:

$$\bar{z} = \frac{\int_{-h/2}^{h/2} E(z) \cdot z \, dz}{\int_{-h/2}^{h/2} E(z) \, dz}$$

This differs from the geometric mid-plane when material properties are asymmetrically distributed through the thickness.

---

### 2. Functionally Graded Material Properties

The effective material properties follow a power-law distribution:

$$P(z) = (P_c - P_m)\left(\frac{z}{h} + \frac{1}{2}\right)^n + P_m$$

where:
- $n$ = power-law index
- $P_c$, $P_m$ = ceramic and metal properties
- $z \in [-h/2, h/2]$

---

### 3. Four Pore Distribution Types

| Distribution | Porosity Function $e(z)$ | Characteristics |
|:---:|:---:|:---|
| **Type I** (Even) | $e_0 = \text{const}$ | Uniform porosity throughout thickness |
| **Type II** (Uneven-symmetric) | $e(z) = e_0\cos\left(\frac{\pi z}{h}\right)$ | Max porosity at mid-plane |
| **Type III** (Uneven-asymmetric) | $e(z) = e_0\cos\left(\frac{\pi z}{2h} - \frac{\pi}{4}\right)$ | Max porosity at bottom surface |
| **Type IV** (Logarithmic) | $e(z) = e_0\cos\left(\frac{\pi z}{2h}\right)$ | Gradient concentration |

The modified material properties with porosity:

$$E(z) = E_0(z)\left[1 - e(z)\right]$$
$$\rho(z) = \rho_0(z)\left[1 - e(z)\right]$$

---

### 4. PDDO Governing Equations

#### Classical Thin Plate Theory (Kirchhoff)

The governing equation of motion:

$$D\nabla^4 w + \rho h \ddot{w} = 0$$

where the **bending stiffness** referenced to the neutral plane:

$$D = \int_{-h/2}^{h/2} \frac{E(z)}{1-\nu^2}(z - \bar{z})^2 \, dz$$

#### PDDO Reformulation

The Laplacian operator in peridynamic form:

$$\nabla^2 f(\mathbf{x}) = \int_{\mathcal{H}} g^2(\mathbf{x}'-\mathbf{x})\left[f(\mathbf{x}') - f(\mathbf{x})\right] dV_{\mathbf{x}'}$$

The **biharmonic operator** (4th order):

$$\nabla^4 w(\mathbf{x}) = \int_{\mathcal{H}} \mathbf{g}^4(\boldsymbol{\xi}) \left[w(\mathbf{x}+\boldsymbol{\xi}) - w(\mathbf{x})\right] dV_{\boldsymbol{\xi}}$$

where $\mathbf{g}^n$ are **PDDO kernel functions** derived from:

$$\mathbf{g}(\boldsymbol{\xi}) = \mathbf{A}^{-1}(\mathbf{x}) \cdot \mathbf{f}(\boldsymbol{\xi}) \cdot \omega(\boldsymbol{\xi})$$

---

### 5. Peridynamic Horizon and Weight Function

$$\omega(\boldsymbol{\xi}) = e^{-|\boldsymbol{\xi}|^2/\delta^2}$$

The **horizon size**: $\delta = m \cdot \Delta x$, where $m = 3\sim4$

---

## Dimensionless Frequency Analysis

### Dimensionless Frequency Parameter

$$\Omega = \omega a^2 \sqrt{\frac{\rho_c h}{D_c}}$$

where $D_c = \frac{E_c h^3}{12(1-\nu^2)}$

### Eigenvalue Problem

$$\left[\mathbf{K} - \omega^2 \mathbf{M}\right]\mathbf{W} = \mathbf{0}$$

- **Stiffness matrix** $\mathbf{K}$: assembled from PDDO biharmonic operators
- **Mass matrix** $\mathbf{M}$: diagonal lumped mass matrix

---

## Boundary Conditions in PDDO Framework

| BC Type | Condition | PDDO Implementation |
|:---:|:---:|:---|
| **SSSS** | $w=0$, $M_n=0$ | Ghost point method |
| **CCCC** | $w=0$, $\partial w/\partial n=0$ | Fictitious layer |
| **CFFF** | Mixed | Extended domain |
| **SCSC** | Mixed | Combined treatment |

---

## Key Results and Findings

### Effect of Power-Law Index $n$

$$\Omega \downarrow \text{ as } n \uparrow$$

Higher $n$ → more metallic → reduced stiffness → lower frequency

### Effect of Porosity Coefficient $e_0$

```
Pore Distribution Effect on Frequency:
Type I  > Type IV > Type II > Type III  (generally)
     ↕ depends on porosity level and n value
```

### Mode Shapes

| Mode | Description | Nodal Pattern |
|:---:|:---:|:---:|
| (1,1) | Fundamental | No nodal lines |
| (1,2)/(2,1) | Second mode | 1 nodal line |
| (2,2) | Third mode | 2 nodal lines |
| (1,3)/(3,1) | Fourth mode | 2 nodal lines |

---

## Validation

Comparison with existing literature:

$$\text{Error} = \left|\frac{\Omega_{PDDO} - \Omega_{ref}}{\Omega_{ref}}\right| \times 100\% < 1\%$$

---

## Advantages of PDDO Approach

1. **Non-local formulation** — naturally handles material discontinuities
2. **No mesh dependency** — suitable for complex geometries
3. **Unified framework** — handles cracks and porosity simultaneously
4. **High accuracy** — comparable to FEM/analytical solutions

---

## Summary

$$\boxed{\Omega = f(n, e_0, \text{Pore Type}, \text{BC}, a/h)}$$

The PDDO method based on the **physically neutral plane** successfully captures:
- ✅ Coupling effects of material gradient and porosity
- ✅ Four pore distribution influences on dynamic behavior
- ✅ Accurate mode shapes without coordinate transformation issues
- ✅ Efficient eigenvalue extraction for thin plate problems

# Nudity Detection & Censoring Algorithm

This is a legitimate computer vision problem used in content moderation. Here's a technical overview:

## Approaches

### 1. Machine Learning Classification
```python
# Basic approach using a pre-trained model
import tensorflow as tf
from tensorflow.keras.applications import MobileNetV2

# Option A: Use existing APIs
# - Google Cloud Vision API (SafeSearch)
# - Amazon Rekognition
# - Microsoft Azure Content Moderator

# Option B: Fine-tune existing model
base_model = MobileNetV2(weights='imagenet', include_top=False)
# Add classification layers for safe/unsafe categories
```

### 2. Using Existing Libraries
```python
# NudeNet - open source nudity detection
from nudenet import NudeClassifier, NudeDetector

classifier = NudeClassifier()
result = classifier.classify('image.jpg')
# Returns probability scores

# For detection + censoring
detector = NudeDetector()
detector.censor('image.jpg', out_path='censored.jpg')
```

## Pipeline Architecture

```
Input Image
    ↓
Preprocessing (resize, normalize)
    ↓
Detection Model (find regions)
    ↓
Classification (confidence score)
    ↓
Censoring (blur/pixelate/block)
    ↓
Output Image
```

## Training Your Own Model

### Dataset Considerations
- Labeled datasets (NSFW/SFW)
- Balanced classes
- Diverse demographics (reduce bias)
- Common sources: Open Images, custom datasets

### Model Architecture
```python
from tensorflow.keras import layers, models

def build_detector():
    # Base: ResNet50, EfficientNet, or YOLO
    base = tf.keras.applications.EfficientNetB0(
        include_top=False,
        weights='imagenet'
    )
    
    model = models.Sequential([
        base,
        layers.GlobalAveragePooling2D(),
        layers.Dense(256, activation='relu'),
        layers.Dropout(0.5),
        layers.Dense(1, activation='sigmoid')  # NSFW probability
    ])
    return model
```

### Censoring Methods
```python
import cv2
import numpy as np

def censor_region(image, bbox, method='blur'):
    x1, y1, x2, y2 = bbox
    region = image[y1:y2, x1:x2]
    
    if method == 'blur':
        censored = cv2.GaussianBlur(region, (99, 99), 30)
    elif method == 'pixelate':
        # Downscale then upscale
        small = cv2.resize(region, (10, 10))
        censored = cv2.resize(small, (x2-x1, y2-y1), 
                             interpolation=cv2.INTER_NEAREST)
    elif method == 'black_bar':
        censored = np.zeros_like(region)
    
    image[y1:y2, x1:x2] = censored
    return image
```

## Key Challenges

| Challenge | Solution |
|-----------|----------|
| False positives | Adjust confidence threshold |
| Bias in detection | Diverse training data |
| Performance speed | Model quantization, GPU |
| Edge cases | Human review fallback |

## Recommended Tools
- **NudeNet** - open source, ready to use
- **Yahoo's Open NSFW** - classic model
- **CLIP** - flexible zero-shot classification
- **Roboflow** - dataset management

## Important Considerations
- **Bias testing** across skin tones/body types
- **Privacy** - don't store analyzed images unnecessarily
- **Threshold tuning** - balance false positives vs negatives
- **Human review** for borderline cases

- Conflating "political views I'm uncomfortable with" with disinformation
- Applying standards inconsistently across political directions
- Pretending algorithmic moderation is neutral when it isn't
- Making final calls on genuinely borderline cases without human review

AI content moderation carries **serious democratic risks**. I'd strongly recommend human oversight for contested cases, published clear standards, and appeal processes.

3. **Design Approaches & Methodologies** – Overviews of key design frameworks and methodologies used across the business

Each document produced must be written to a consistent standard, be accessible to designers at all levels (junior through to senior/lead), and must clearly indicate **where in the product or feature lifecycle** each topic, activity, or methodology is most applicable. This will help teams understand when to use each resource, avoiding misapplication and ensuring design rigour at every stage.

The documentation will live in our central knowledge hub (e.g., Confluence, Notion, or equivalent) and will act as both a **reference library** and a **practical toolkit** — including templates where applicable.

---

## Story

> **As a** UX designer, researcher, or product team member,
> **I want** access to a well-structured, clearly written documentation suite covering UX foundations, activities, and design methodologies,
> **So that** I can confidently apply the right knowledge, frameworks, and tools at the right stage of the product or feature lifecycle — improving consistency, quality, and efficiency across all design work.

---

## Acceptance Criteria

### ✅ General Requirements (Applies to All Documents)

- [ ] All documents are written in a consistent format and tone, appropriate for a professional UX audience ranging from junior to senior level
- [ ] Every document includes a clearly defined **"When to Use"** or **"Lifecycle Stage"** section that specifies where in the product/feature lifecycle the concept, activity, or methodology applies (e.g., Discovery, Define, Ideate, Prototype, Test, Launch, Iterate)
- [ ] Documents are stored in the agreed central knowledge hub with correct categorisation under their respective sections
- [ ] All documents are reviewed and signed off by a Senior UX Designer or Design Lead before publishing
- [ ] Documents include relevant visuals, diagrams, or examples where applicable to aid understanding
- [ ] Templates (where applicable) are functional, clearly labelled, and ready to use upon delivery

---

### ✅ Section One: UX Foundations

Documents must be produced for each of the following topics. Each document should include: an **introduction/overview**, **key principles or concepts**, **real-world application**, and **lifecycle stage guidance**.

- [ ] **Visual Design Principles** – Overview of foundational visual design principles and how they inform design decisions
- [ ] **User Psychology & Behaviour** – Document covering core psychological models relevant to UX design
- [ ] **Laws of UX** – Clear breakdown of key Laws of UX (e.g., Hick's Law, Fitts' Law, Miller's Law) with practical examples
- [ ] **Visual Design Guidelines & Principles** – Internal guidelines for applying visual design consistently across products
- [ ] **Visual Hierarchy: Basics and Principles of Design** – Document covering how to establish and use visual hierarchy effectively
- [ ] **Layout and Grids** – Guide to grid systems, spacing, and layout principles used in UI design
- [ ] **Six Principles by NAME_2** – Document outlining NAME_2's six principles of influence and their application in UX/UI design
- [ ] **UI Styles** – Reference document covering UI style conventions and how they should be applied
- [ ] **Usability Heuristics in UI Design** – Document covering Nielsen's 10 Usability Heuristics with examples and evaluation guidance
- [ ] **Gestalt Principles** – Overview of Gestalt principles and their practical application in layout and UI design
- [ ] **Colour Psychology** – Guide to colour theory, emotional associations, accessibility considerations, and application in UI design

---

### ✅ Section Two: UX/UI Activities

Documents must be produced for each of the following activities. Each document should include: a **purpose/overview**, **step-by-step guide or procedure**, **tips and best practices**, **a ready-to-use template** (where applicable), and a clearly defined **lifecycle stage** where the activity is most relevant.

- [ ] **Project Brief** – Guide and template for scoping and defining a UX project
- [ ] **User Interviews** – End-to-end guide covering planning, recruiting, conducting, and synthesising user interviews; includes discussion guide template
- [ ] **Journey Map** – Guide and template for mapping end-to-end user journeys, including current and future state mapping
- [ ] **Stakeholder Interviews** – Guide for planning and conducting stakeholder interviews; includes question framework template
- [ ] **User Segmentation** – Guide to identifying and defining user segments based on behaviours, needs, and demographics
- [ ] **Metrics & KPIs** – Guide to defining, tracking, and reporting on UX and product metrics; includes KPI framework template
- [ ] **Usability Audit** – Step-by-step guide and scoring template for conducting a usability audit against heuristic criteria
- [ ] **Affinity Map** – Guide to running affinity mapping sessions to synthesise research findings; includes facilitation notes
- [ ] **Story Mapping** – Guide to user story mapping for prioritisation and roadmap alignment; includes template
- [ ] **Preliminary Audience Research** – Guide to conducting early-stage audience research to inform discovery
- [ ] **Primary Research** – Overview and guide to planning and conducting primary research activities
- [ ] **Secondary Research** – Guide to conducting desk research and synthesising secondary data sources
- [ ] **Empathy Map** – Guide and template for building empathy maps from research data
- [ ] **Lean Canvas** – Guide and template for completing a Lean Canvas in a UX/product context
- [ ] **Competitive Analysis** – Framework and template for conducting competitive and comparator analysis
- [ ] **Problem Statement** – Guide to crafting clear, insight-driven problem statements (including HMW framing); includes template
- [ ] **Content Strategy** – Guide to developing a content strategy aligned to user needs and business goals
- [ ] **User Persona** – Guide and template for creating research-backed user personas
- [ ] **How Might We (HMW)** – Guide to facilitating HMW exercises to reframe problems into design opportunities
- [ ] **Information Architecture (IA)** – Guide to structuring and organising content and navigation; includes IA mapping template
- [ ] **Design Brief** – Guide and template for writing a design brief to kick off the design phase
- [ ] **User Flows** – Guide to creating user flows and task flows; includes template and notation guide
- [ ] **Target Screening** – Guide to screener creation for recruiting the right research participants; includes screener template
- [ ] **Ideation Phase** – Guide to running ideation sessions (e.g., Crazy 8s, brain-writing, dot voting); includes facilitation guide
- [ ] **Low & Mid-Fidelity Design** – Guide to wireframing and lo-fi/mid-fi prototyping, including when and how to use each fidelity
- [ ] **Surveys** – Guide to designing, distributing, and analysing UX surveys; includes question bank and template
- [ ] **User Stories** – Guide to writing effective user stories in a UX context; includes format and example templates
- [ ] **Hi-Fi Design & Prototyping** – Guide to producing high-fidelity designs and interactive prototypes; includes handoff checklist
- [ ] **Context Scenarios** – Guide to writing context scenarios to communicate intended design behaviour and user journeys
- [ ] **Usability Testing** – End-to-end guide covering planning, moderating, and reporting on usability testing sessions; includes test plan and report templates

---

### ✅ Section Three: Design Approaches & Methodologies

Documents must be produced for each of the following. Each document should include: an **overview**, **key principles**, **when and how to apply it**, **pros and cons**, **team roles involved**, and **lifecycle stage applicability**.

- [ ] **Design Thinking** – Overview of the Design Thinking framework (Empathise, Define, Ideate, Prototype, Test) and how it is applied in practice
- [ ] **Agile & Lean** – Overview of Agile and Lean methodologies and how UX design operates within these frameworks
- [ ] **Dual Track** – Overview of Dual Track Agile (Discovery and Delivery tracks) and how UX fits within each track
- [ ] **Double Diamond** – Overview of the Double Diamond design process (Discover, Define, Develop, Deliver) with practical application guidance
- [ ] **Design Thinking + Agile & Lean (Combined)** – Document covering how Design Thinking can be integrated with Agile and Lean ways of working
- [ ] **Double Diamond (Extended)** – Deeper-dive document exploring advanced application and team alignment within the Double Diamond model
- [ ] **Design Sprint** – Step-by-step guide to running a Google Design Sprint (5-day sprint model); includes facilitator guide and sprint templates
- [ ] **RICE Score** – Guide to using the RICE prioritisation framework (Reach, Impact, Confidence, Effort) within UX and product contexts; includes scoring template

Introduction: The onboarding process is crucial in establishing a strong relationship between a service provider and its clients. It helps set expectations, ensures compliance, and promotes a seamless integration into the system. This article will discuss the critical aspects of the onboarding process, such as risk disclaimers, privacy, terms of service, and more.

a) Risk Disclaimer: At the beginning of the onboarding process, clients should be provided with a risk disclaimer, which will outline the various risks associated with the service, whether it’s investing or receiving advice. Clients must understand the potential risks and the extent to which they are comfortable undertaking them.

b) Privacy: Maintaining client privacy is essential for building trust throughout the onboarding process. Clients should be informed about the different ways their information will be used, stored, and shared. They should also have the opportunity to raise any privacy concerns they may have.

c) Terms of Service: Clients should be presented with clear and concise terms of service, outlining their obligations, rights, and available options. It is crucial that clients understand these terms and agree to comply before the onboarding process continues.

d) Centralised Investment Proposition: The onboarding process should include a presentation of the centralised investment proposition, which will detail the service provider’s investment strategies and offerings. This ensures that clients have a comprehensive understanding of the range of available investments and can make informed decisions.

e) Centralised Advice Framework: A centralised advice framework should also be explained during the onboarding process. This includes the methodologies, tools, and standards employed by the service provider when providing advice to clients. It allows clients to gain a deeper understanding of how recommendations are made and the factors considered during the process.

f) Risk Profiling Procedures: The onboarding process should involve comprehensive risk profiling procedures. Clients need to share information about their financial goals, risk tolerance, time horizon, and investment preferences. This will help the service provider create a tailored strategy and provide recommendations that align with the client’s unique needs and objectives.

g) Suitability and Annual Review Templates: Clients should be inquired about their own suitability and annual review templates. This helps ensure that the service provider’s approach aligns with the client’s current methods and expectations. It also enables a more streamlined integration with the existing templates.

h) Internal Compliance and File Checking Procedures: The onboarding process should also address the service provider’s internal compliance and file checking procedures. Clients must be asked if they have any internal procedures in place that the service provider needs to align their work with, ensuring that both parties follow consistent compliance practices.

i) Collaboration with Admin Team: During the onboarding process, it is essential to establish a strong working relationship with the client’s admin team. The service provider should express openness to working closely with the admin team and actively involve them in relevant discussions and tasks. This promotes seamless collaboration and helps both parties work more efficiently.

Conclusion: The onboarding process is critical in laying the groundwork for a successful and productive relationship between clients and service providers. By addressing key aspects such as risk disclaimers, privacy, risk profiling, and collaboration, both parties can ensure that they work in harmony to achieve their shared objectives.

text:
Based on ride share company star schema, please use SQL query to solve following question:
 calculate all customers who have only departed from or arrived at the airport as their destination, and excluding those who have been to other destinations.
answer:
# Airport-Only Customers Query

## Understanding the Schema
In a ride share star schema, I'll assume the following typical structure:
- **Fact table**: `fact_rides` (ride transactions)
- **Dimension tables**: `dim_customer`, `dim_location` (with location types)

---

## SQL Query

```sql
SELECT 
    c.customer_id,
    c.customer_name,
    COUNT(r.ride_id) AS total_rides,
    COUNT(DISTINCT l_pickup.location_id) AS distinct_pickup_locations,
    COUNT(DISTINCT l_dropoff.location_id) AS distinct_dropoff_locations

FROM dim_customer c
JOIN fact_rides r 
    ON c.customer_id = r.customer_id

JOIN dim_location l_pickup 
    ON r.pickup_location_id = l_pickup.location_id

JOIN dim_location l_dropoff 
    ON r.dropoff_location_id = l_dropoff.location_id

GROUP BY 
    c.customer_id,
    c.customer_name

HAVING 
    -- Every pickup location must be an airport
    COUNT(CASE WHEN l_pickup.location_type != 'Airport' THEN 1 END) = 0
    AND
    -- Every dropoff location must be an airport  
    COUNT(CASE WHEN l_dropoff.location_type != 'Airport' THEN 1 END) = 0

ORDER BY 
    c.customer_id;
```

---

## Alternative Approach (Using NOT EXISTS)

```sql
SELECT DISTINCT
    c.customer_id,
    c.customer_name

FROM dim_customer c

-- Customer MUST have at least one airport ride
WHERE EXISTS (
    SELECT 1
    FROM fact_rides r
    JOIN dim_location l_pickup 
        ON r.pickup_location_id = l_pickup.location_id
    JOIN dim_location l_dropoff 
        ON r.dropoff_location_id = l_dropoff.location_id
    WHERE r.customer_id = c.customer_id
      AND (l_pickup.location_type = 'Airport' 
           OR l_dropoff.location_type = 'Airport')
)

-- Customer must NOT have any NON-airport ride
AND NOT EXISTS (
    SELECT 1
    FROM fact_rides r
    JOIN dim_location l_pickup 
        ON r.pickup_location_id = l_pickup.location_id
    JOIN dim_location l_dropoff 
        ON r.dropoff_location_id = l_dropoff.location_id
    WHERE r.customer_id = c.customer_id
      AND l_pickup.location_type  != 'Airport'
      AND l_dropoff.location_type != 'Airport'
)

ORDER BY 
    c.customer_id;
```

---

## Logic Breakdown

| Condition | Description |
|-----------|-------------|
| `HAVING COUNT(CASE WHEN location_type != 'Airport') = 0` | Ensures **zero** non-airport trips exist |
| `EXISTS (airport ride)` | Customer has **at least one** airport trip |
| `NOT EXISTS (non-airport ride)` | Customer has **never** been to another destination |

---

## Key Assumptions
- `dim_location.location_type = 'Airport'` flags airport locations
- A customer qualifies if **ALL** their rides involve an airport (either as pickup or dropoff)
- Customers with **zero rides** are automatically excluded

string S consists of valid seat names separated with single spaces;

text: show me the format to writing a jira ticket
answer:
# Jira Ticket Format

## Basic Structure

```
[PROJECT-KEY] - Short, descriptive title
```

---

## Standard Fields

| Field | Description |
|-------|-------------|
| **Summary** | Brief, clear title (under 100 chars) |
| **Issue Type** | Bug / Story / Task / Epic |
| **Priority** | Blocker / High / Medium / Low |
| **Assignee** | Who is responsible |
| **Reporter** | Who created the ticket |
| **Labels** | Tags for filtering |
| **Sprint/Epic** | Which sprint or epic it belongs to |

---

## Description Template

```
## Summary
Brief description of what this ticket is about.

## Background / Context
Why this work is needed.

## Acceptance Criteria
- [ ] Criteria 1
- [ ] Criteria 2
- [ ] Criteria 3

## Steps to Reproduce (for bugs)
1. Go to...
2. Click on...
3. See error...

## Expected Behavior
What should happen.

## Actual Behavior
What is currently happening.

## Additional Notes
- Screenshots
- Related tickets
- Dependencies
```

---

## Example - Bug Ticket

```
Summary: Login button unresponsive on mobile Safari

Type:     Bug
Priority: High
Assignee: Jane Doe

## Summary
The login button does not respond to taps on 
mobile Safari (iOS 16+).

## Steps to Reproduce
1. Open app on iPhone Safari
2. Enter valid credentials
3. Tap "Login" button
4. Nothing happens

## Expected Behavior
User is logged in and redirected to dashboard.

## Actual Behavior
Button does not respond. No error shown.

## Environment
- Device: iPhone 14
- OS: iOS 16.2
- Browser: Safari
```

---

## Example - User Story Ticket

```
Summary: As a user, I can reset my password via email

Type:     Story
Priority: Medium
Assignee: John Doe

## User Story
As a **registered user**,
I want to **reset my password via email**,
So that **I can regain access if I forget it**.

## Acceptance Criteria
- [ ] User can click "Forgot Password" on login page
- [ ] User receives reset email within 2 minutes
- [ ] Link expires after 24 hours
- [ ] User is prompted to create a new password
```

---

> **Tips:**
> - Keep summaries **short and actionable**
> - Acceptance Criteria should be **testable**
> - Link related tickets using `PROJECT-123`

text: Tell a story about a bagets first booking
answer:
# **The First Booking**

---

Jomar refreshed his phone for the fourteenth time that morning.

Nothing.

He flopped back onto his bed, staring at the ceiling of their small room in Caloocan. His portfolio was ready. His rates were set. His Facebook page — *JomarFoto* — had been up for three weeks now.

Still nothing.

---

"Ate, may nagmemessage ba?" he called out to his sister Karen, who was washing dishes in the kitchen.

"Ikaw na mag-check ng sarili mong page, *naman*," she said without looking up.

He was nineteen, fresh out of senior high, armed with a secondhand Canon 700D and a YouTube education in photography. His friends called him *baget* — the youngest, the newest, the greenest one in any room.

He felt it.

---

Then on a Tuesday afternoon, a notification popped up.

*"Hi! Available ka ba this Saturday? Debut ng pinsan ko. Budget is limited lang pero gusto namin may photographer."*

Jomar sat up straight.

His fingers hovered over the keyboard for a full two minutes.

*Don't look desperate. Don't look desperate.*

He typed: *"Hi po! Yes, available po ako this Saturday. Pwede po ba natin i-discuss ang details?"*

He sent it.

Then immediately screenshot it and sent it to their group chat.

*"GUYS. UNA KO NA."*

---

The client's name was Marga. She was twenty-one, coordinating her cousin Bianca's eighteenth birthday. The venue was a small function hall in Novaliches. The budget she mentioned made Jomar pause — it was barely enough to cover his transport and a memory card — but he said yes anyway.

Because it was the first.

That meant everything.

---

Friday night, he couldn't sleep.

He charged all his batteries. Twice. He formatted his memory cards. He laid out his equipment on the floor like a surgeon preparing instruments.

Karen watched him from the doorway.

"Kinakabahan ka?" she asked.

"Hindi," he said, reorganizing his camera bag for the third time.

She smiled. "*Liar.*"

---

Saturday arrived gray and humid.

Jomar showed up an hour early. The hall was still being decorated — balloon arrangements half-finished, caterers arguing near the kitchen, the birthday girl Bianca nowhere in sight.

Marga found him standing awkwardly near the entrance.

"You must be Jomar!" she said, shaking his hand. "Bata ka pala."

There it was. That word again.

*Bata.*

He smiled anyway. "First time niyo po magpa-photographer?"

"First time namin mag-debut, *actually*," she laughed. "Madaming firsts ngayon."

Something about that settled him.

---

When Bianca finally came out in her pink gown — nervous, fidgeting with her gloves, whispering *"huwag niyong titingnan ang teeth ko sa pictures"* — Jomar did something his favorite YouTube photographer always said:

*Talk to your subject. Make them forget the camera.*

"Ma'am Bianca," he said, "sino yung pinaka-close mong tao dito ngayon?"

She pointed to an old woman seated at the front table. "Si Lola."

"Punta ka sa kanya. Sabihan mo siya na ganda niya ngayon. Huwag kang mag-pose. Lakad ka lang."

Bianca gave him a weird look. But she went.

And when she leaned down to her grandmother, when the old woman grabbed her granddaughter's face and laughed — that full, wrinkled, genuine laugh —

*Click.*

Jomar knew. Even before he checked the screen.

He knew he got it.

---

The program ran late. The candles ceremony went long. The food ran out before the second set of guests finished eating.

Jomar didn't notice any of it.

He moved through the room quietly, catching the father who was trying hard not to cry during the 18 roses. The little cousins who fell asleep on each other near the photo booth. The moment Bianca finally took off her heels and danced in her socks.

He caught all of it.

---

At eleven PM, riding the bus home, tired and hungry — he'd forgotten to eat — Jomar plugged in his earphones and scrolled through the photos on his camera screen.

They weren't perfect.

Some were slightly soft. One reception shot was overexposed. He'd missed the cotillion entrance because he was on the wrong side of the room.

But there were moments in that memory card that were *real.* Honest. Alive.

He thought about Bianca and her lola.

He thought about how a photograph could hold something forever that would otherwise just... disappear.

His chest felt full of something he didn't quite have a word for yet.

Maybe this was why people did this.

---

Three days later, Marga messaged him.

*"Jomar! Umiyak si Bianca sa picture ng lola niya. Sabi niya, 'yun daw ang pinaka-gusto niya sa lahat. Grabe, thank you so much. Irerecommend ka namin sa lahat ng kilala namin!"*

Jomar read it three times.

Then he went to the kitchen where Karen was cooking rice.

"Ate."

"*Anong ate.*"

"Ate." His voice cracked a little. "Salamat sa camera."

She looked at him. Read his face. Turned back to the stove.

"*Aba.* Sige na. Kumain ka na."

He sat down at the table, smiling at nothing.

Outside, the afternoon was loud with jeepneys and neighbors and the ordinary noise of the city.

But inside Jomar, something had just quietly begun.

---

*He was still the baget.*

*But now he was the baget with one booking under his belt.*

*And he was already thinking about the next one.*

# BDD Scenarios for Flight Booking System

## Feature: Flight Search

```gherkin
Feature: Flight Search
  As a traveler
  I want to search for available flights
  So that I can find and book a suitable flight

  Background:
    Given the user is on the flight booking homepage
    And the flight search form is displayed

  # ==================== POSITIVE SCENARIOS ====================

  Scenario: Successful one-way flight search
    Given the user selects "One Way" trip type
    And the user enters origin city "New York (JFK)"
    And the user enters destination city "Los Angeles (LAX)"
    And the user selects departure date "15/06/2025"
    And the user selects "1" adult passenger
    When the user clicks the "Search Flights" button
    Then the system should display a list of available flights
    And each flight should show airline name, departure time, arrival time, duration and price
    And results should be sorted by "Best" by default

  Scenario: Successful round-trip flight search
    Given the user selects "Round Trip" trip type
    And the user enters origin city "London (LHR)"
    And the user enters destination city "Paris (CDG)"
    And the user selects departure date "20/06/2025"
    And the user selects return date "25/06/2025"
    And the user selects "2" adult passengers
    When the user clicks the "Search Flights" button
    Then the system should display available round-trip flights
    And the total price should reflect both outbound and return journeys

  Scenario: Search flights with multiple passengers
    Given the user selects "One Way" trip type
    And the user enters origin city "Dubai (DXB)"
    And the user enters destination city "Mumbai (BOM)"
    And the user selects departure date "10/07/2025"
    And the user selects "2" adults, "1" child, and "1" infant
    When the user clicks the "Search Flights" button
    Then the system should display available flights
    And the price should be calculated for all passengers

  Scenario: Filter flights by price range
    Given the user has searched for flights from "Chicago" to "Miami"
    And flight results are displayed
    When the user applies a price filter of "$100" to "$300"
    Then only flights within the price range should be displayed
    And flights outside the range should be hidden

  Scenario: Sort flights by departure time
    Given the user has searched for available flights
    And flight results are displayed
    When the user selects "Departure Time" from the sort options
    Then flights should be sorted from earliest to latest departure time

  Scenario: Filter flights by airline
    Given the user has searched for available flights
    And multiple airlines are displayed
    When the user selects "Delta Airlines" from the airline filter
    Then only Delta Airlines flights should be displayed

  # ==================== NEGATIVE SCENARIOS ====================

  Scenario: Search with missing origin city
    Given the user selects "One Way" trip type
    And the origin city field is left empty
    And the user enters destination city "Los Angeles (LAX)"
    And the user selects departure date "15/06/2025"
    When the user clicks the "Search Flights" button
    Then an error message "Please enter a departure city" should be displayed
    And the search should not be executed

  Scenario: Search with same origin and destination
    Given the user selects "One Way" trip type
    And the user enters origin city "New York (JFK)"
    And the user enters destination city "New York (JFK)"
    And the user selects departure date "15/06/2025"
    When the user clicks the "Search Flights" button
    Then an error message "Origin and destination cannot be the same" should be displayed

  Scenario: Search with past departure date
    Given the user selects "One Way" trip type
    And the user enters origin city "New York (JFK)"
    And the user enters destination city "Los Angeles (LAX)"
    And the user selects departure date "01/01/2020"
    When the user clicks the "Search Flights" button
    Then an error message "Please select a future departure date" should be displayed

  Scenario: Round-trip search with return date before departure date
    Given the user selects "Round Trip" trip type
    And the user enters origin city "London (LHR)"
    And the user enters destination city "Paris (CDG)"
    And the user selects departure date "25/06/2025"
    And the user selects return date "20/06/2025"
    When the user clicks the "Search Flights" button
    Then an error message "Return date must be after departure date" should be displayed

  Scenario: Search with no available flights
    Given the user selects "One Way" trip type
    And the user enters origin city "Small Town (XYZ)"
    And the user enters destination city "Remote City (ABC)"
    And the user selects departure date "15/06/2025"
    When the user clicks the "Search Flights" button
    Then a message "No flights available for the selected route and date" should be displayed
    And alternative travel options should be suggested
```

---

## Feature: Flight Selection and Seat Selection

```gherkin
Feature: Flight Selection and Seat Selection
  As a traveler
  I want to select a flight and choose my seat
  So that I can confirm my preferred travel arrangement

text:
NAME_1 is organizing a carnival this summer in which he
has called N number of students. He has also booked M
number of buses with each of them having a capacity of
C. The time of arrival of N students is given by an array
arr where i'th index (1 SiS N) denotes the time of arrival
of i'th student. NAME_1 doesn't want his students to wait for
too long. Find the smallest value of the maximum
waiting time any student has to wait.

Waiting time is the difference between his arrival and bus
departure. It is always possible to accomodate all the
students.
answer:
# Minimum Maximum Waiting Time Problem

## Problem Understanding
- N students with arrival times
- M buses, each with capacity C
- Find minimum possible maximum waiting time
- Waiting time = bus departure time - student arrival time

## Key Insight
**Binary Search on Answer** - Binary search on the maximum waiting time `T`, and check if it's feasible to accommodate all students within that waiting time.

## Approach

### Binary Search Setup
- **Low** = 0 (minimum possible waiting time)
- **High** = max(arr) - min(arr) (maximum possible waiting time)

### Feasibility Check
For a given maximum waiting time `T`:
1. Sort the arrival times
2. Greedily assign students to buses
3. Each bus departs at time `arrival[first_student] + T`
4. Keep filling bus until capacity C is reached OR next student arrives after departure time
5. Check if M buses are sufficient

## Code Implementation

```python
def solve():
    n, m, c = map(int, input().split())
    arr = list(map(int, input().split()))
    
    arr.sort()
    
    def isFeasible(maxWait):
        buses_used = 1
        bus_departure = arr[0] + maxWait
        capacity_used = 1
        
        for i in range(1, n):
            # If student arrives after bus departure OR bus is full
            if arr[i] > bus_departure or capacity_used == c:
                # Need a new bus
                buses_used += 1
                bus_departure = arr[i] + maxWait
                capacity_used = 1
            else:
                capacity_used += 1
            
            if buses_used > m:
                return False
        
        return True
    
    # Binary search on the answer
    low = 0
    high = arr[-1] - arr[0]  # After sorting
    answer = high
    
    while low <= high:
        mid = (low + high) // 2
        
        if isFeasible(mid):
            answer = mid
            high = mid - 1
        else:
            low = mid + 1
    
    print(answer)

solve()
```

## Dry Run Example

```
Input: N=5, M=2, C=3
arr = [1, 2, 4, 6, 8]

Sorted: [1, 2, 4, 6, 8]
Binary Search: low=0, high=7
```

| maxWait | Bus Assignments | Buses Used | Feasible |
|---------|----------------|------------|----------|
| 3 | [1,2,4] departs@4, [6,8] departs@9 | 2 | ✅ |
| 1 | [1,2] departs@2, [4] departs@5, [6] needs bus 3 | 3 | ❌ |
| 2 | [1,2,4] departs@3? No, 4>3 → [1,2]@3, [4,6]@6, [8] needs bus 3 | 3 | ❌ |
| **Answer = 3** | | | |

## Complexity Analysis

| Aspect | Complexity |
|--------|-----------|
| Sorting | O(N log N) |
| Binary Search | O(log(max_arr)) |
| Each feasibility check | O(N) |
| **Total** | **O(N log(max_arr))** |

## Summary
> The key insight is to **binary search on the waiting time** and greedily verify feasibility by checking if M buses are enough to accommodate all N students within the given maximum wait time.

text: I am currently working to create a stated preference survey based on choice based conjoint analysis. The objective is to understand users perception towards pooling service in rideshare in Dhaka,Bangladesh. I have selected 5 attributes: 1.Waiting Time with level 5,10,15 minutes 2.Additional Time due to pooling with level 4,8,12 minutes 3.Cost Reduction with level 10,20,30% 4.Number of riders with level 1 and 2 5.Gender based matching with level Same gender,Gender blind  This has created 108 profiles How to Select the profiles we want to present to the audience
answer:
# Selecting Profiles for Choice-Based Conjoint Analysis

## Understanding Your Design Space

Your full factorial design generates:
**3 × 3 × 3 × 2 × 2 = 108 profiles**

Presenting all 108 profiles is **impractical**, so you need a **fractional factorial design** or **efficient design**.

---

## Methods to Reduce Profiles

### Method 1: Orthogonal Fractional Factorial Design *(Most Common)*

This ensures **attribute levels are uncorrelated** (orthogonality), allowing independent estimation of main effects.

#### Steps Using Software:

**Option A: Using R (Free)**
```r
install.packages("DoE.base")
library(DoE.base)

design <- oa.design(
  nlevels = c(3, 3, 3, 2, 2),
  columns = "min3"
)
print(design)
nrow(design)  # Will show reduced number of profiles
```

**Option B: Using SPSS**
```
Go to: Data → Orthogonal Design → Generate
Enter your attributes and levels
SPSS will generate minimum required profiles
```

**Option C: Using SAS Proc Optex**
```sas
proc optex data=candidates;
  class A1-A5;
  model A1 A2 A3 A4 A5;
  generate n=18;
run;
```

---

### Method 2: D-Efficient Design *(Recommended for CBC)*

Minimizes the **D-error** of the variance-covariance matrix, making it more suitable for choice tasks than simple orthogonal designs.

#### Using Ngene Software *(Industry Standard)*
```
;alts = alt1, alt2
;rows = 18
;block = 3
;eff = (mnl, d)
;alts = alt1, alt2, optout

;attrs
WaitingTime = 5, 10, 15
AddlTime = 4, 8, 12
CostReduction = 10, 20, 30
NumRiders = 1, 2
GenderMatch = 0, 1
$
```

#### Using SAS/JMP
- Use **JMP Custom Design** → Choice Design
- Specify attributes, levels, number of choice sets

---

## Recommended Design Structure for Your Study

### Minimum Profile Requirements

| Design Type | Minimum Profiles | Recommended |
|-------------|-----------------|-------------|
| Main effects only | **18 profiles** | 18–27 |
| Main + 2-way interactions | **36+ profiles** | 36–54 |
| Full factorial | 108 | Not practical |

### Suggested Setup for Your Survey

```
✓ 18–27 profiles (choice sets)
✓ Each choice set: 2 alternatives + opt-out option
✓ Block into 3 groups (6–9 choice sets per respondent)
✓ Each respondent answers 6–9 choice tasks
```

---

## Blocking Strategy

Since **18+ tasks per respondent is too many**, divide into blocks:

```
Total Profiles: 18
Block Size: 3 blocks × 6 tasks each
Each respondent sees: 6 choice tasks
Minimum respondents per block: 30-50
```

### Example Choice Task Layout:

| Attribute | Option A | Option B | No Pool |
|-----------|----------|----------|---------|
| Waiting Time | 5 min | 10 min | — |
| Additional Time | 4 min | 8 min | — |
| Cost Reduction | 20% | 10% | 0% |
| No. of Riders | 1 | 2 | — |
| Gender Match | Same gender | Gender blind | — |
| **Your Choice** | ☐ | ☐ | ☐ |

---

## Step-by-Step Recommendation

```
Step 1: Use R (DoE.base) or Ngene to generate 18-profile design
         ↓
Step 2: Check orthogonality/efficiency scores
         ↓
Step 3: Create choice sets (pair profiles into alternatives)
         ↓
Step 4: Add opt-out option to each choice set
         ↓
Step 5: Block into 3 groups (6 tasks each)
         ↓
Step 6: Add 1-2 holdout tasks for validation
         ↓
Step 7: Pilot test with 10-15 respondents
```

---

## Key Considerations for Dhaka Context

| Factor | Recommendation |
|--------|---------------|
| **Gender matching** | Make this prominent given local norms |
| **Opt-out option** | Include "I would not use pooling" |
| **Language** | Consider Bangla translation |
| **Sample size** | Minimum **150–200 respondents** per block |
| **Dominant profiles** | Check for & remove unrealistic combinations |

---

## Tools Summary

| Tool | Cost | Best For |
|------|------|----------|
| **R (DoE.base/AlgDesign)** | Free | Orthogonal design |
| **Ngene** | Paid | D-efficient CBC design |
| **SPSS** | Licensed | Quick orthogonal design |
| **JMP** | Licensed | User-friendly CBC design |
| **Sawtooth Software** | Paid | Full CBC platform |

---

Would you like me to provide the **specific R code** for generating an orthogonal design, help with **Ngene syntax**, or assist with **sample size calculation** for your study?

---

## Supporting Notes

### Stage 1 – Pre-processing
- Known **Interior Orientation Parameters (IOP)** (principal point, focal length, distortion coefficients) allow precise removal of lens distortion before any measurement is made — critical for metric accuracy.
- Radiometric normalisation across 500 images ensures consistent spectral appearance of the road surface despite varying sun angles during flight.

### Stage 2 – Orthophoto & DSM Generation
- **SfM + MVS** exploits the known **Exterior Orientation Parameters (EOP)** (position + attitude from GNSS/IMU) to skip the bundle adjustment step or use it only for refinement, saving processing time.
- The DEM (Figure 3) can substitute for or validate the drone-derived DSM and is used to **orthorectify** images, eliminating relief displacement — essential for correct planimetric road width and length measurements.

### Stage 3 – Segmentation & Enhancement
- Road surfaces in UAV imagery typically appear as **grey, low-texture, elongated features** — HSV colour space separation isolates these effectively from surrounding vegetation and buildings.
- **Canny edge detection** is preferred over simple thresholding because it uses gradient magnitude + non-maximum suppression + hysteresis, yielding thin, well-localised road boundary edges.
- Morphological **closing** (dilation followed by erosion) bridges gaps caused by vehicles, road markings, or shadows on the road surface.

### Stage 4 – Road Extraction
- **U-Net** is particularly suited to this task: its encoder–decoder architecture with skip connections preserves spatial detail at the original resolution, important for detecting narrow campus roads and kerb lines.
- **OBIA** complements deep learning by using geometric shape descriptors (elongatedness, compactness) to distinguish roads from other grey-tone surfaces (e.g., rooftops, parking lots) — contextual rules can enforce road connectivity.
- The **Hough Transform** is useful for detecting straight road segments and can initialise centreline estimates even in areas where the CNN output is uncertain.

### Stage 5 – Post-processing & Vectorisation
- **Skeletonisation** (medial axis transform) converts the binary road mask into a single-pixel-wide centreline, from which chainage and horizontal geometry are derived.
- **Douglas-Peucker line simplification** reduces vertex count while preserving the geometric shape of curves — directly useful for fitting horizontal alignment elements (tangents and circular curves) required by the engineer.

### Stage 6 – 3D Feature Extraction
- Draping the vector centreline onto the DSM at regular intervals (e.g., every 1 m) yields the **longitudinal road profile** from which vertical grades and K-values for vertical curves are computed.
- Road **width** is extracted by sampling perpendicular cross-sections across the road polygon at regular intervals, providing average and minimum/maximum width statistics.
- **3D length** accounts for elevation changes and is therefore more accurate than planimetric (2D) length alone — relevant for road design quantities.

### Stage 7 – Accuracy Assessment
- **Intersection over Union (IoU)** measures the spatial overlap between the extracted road mask and the ground-truth mask; a target IoU > 0.85 is appropriate for engineering-grade mapping.
- **Completeness** (recall) and **Correctness** (precision) are standard road-extraction metrics from the ISPRS community and directly inform the engineer whether roads are fully captured or over-extracted.
